title: Making a leather wristband with a snap fastener
subtitle: Cut and finish a strap from vegetable-tanned leather and fit press-stud snap fasteners for a wristband
excerpt: How to cut a leather wristband to size, punch the adjustment holes, finish the edges, and set a pair of press-stud snap fasteners. No sewing required.
sourceNotes: Traditional leather craft practice. Period saddlery and harness manuals (pre-1928 public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: A four-part metal fastener: a stud cap, a stud socket, an eyelet cap, and an eyelet socket. The cap and socket halves are set through a hole in the leather from front and back respectively using a setting tool and hammer. The two halves snap together and pull apart cleanly. Sized in line and metric; 15 mm is the standard for a leather wristband.

content.text: are set through a punched hole in the leather using a hammer and a small setting punch. The wristband itself is a single rectangle of leather with a rounded end, a row of adjustment holes at the other end, and two snaps: one on the top face and one on the bottom. The adjustment holes give several fit positions.

Measure your wrist circumference. For a comfortable wristband, cut a strap 20 mm wide and roughly 40 mm longer than the wrist measurement (this gives overlap for the snap fastener). Use the utility knife against a metal ruler on a hard cutting board. Cut straight edges; round one end with craft scissors following a template if desired. The strap thickness should be 2 to 3 mm: thick enough to hold the snap firmly, light enough to wear comfortably.
Mark and punch the adjustment holes

At the rounded end of the strap, mark a row of three to five holes centred on the strap width, spaced 10 mm apart, starting 15 mm from the end. Punch the holes with a single-hole revolving punch or a drive punch at 4 mm diameter. These are the adjustment holes that the stud passes through for sizing.

Bevel the top edges of the strap with an edge beveller (or sand lightly with 180-grit sandpaper) to remove the sharp right-angle. Burnish the edges by rubbing firmly with a wooden edge burnisher, a wooden dowel, or the back of a toothbrush with a small amount of saddle soap. The burnishing compresses and seals the flesh side fibres at the edge for a clean finish.

Mark the snap position on the square end of the strap 10 mm from the end and centred on the strap width. Punch a hole with a drive punch at the diameter specified for the snap (usually 5 to 6 mm for a 15 mm snap). Insert the socket half of the snap through the hole from the grain side and position the cap below on the flesh side. Set the cap onto the socket using the setter punch and the claw hammer: two or three firm hammer blows. Repeat on the face of the strap for the stud half of the snap at a position that aligns correctly with the adjustment holes.

attrs.symptom: Snap pulls out of the leather after a few uses
attrs.cause: Leather too thin for the snap size, or snap was not fully set (cap not fully compressed onto socket).
attrs.fix: Use 2.5 mm or thicker leather. Re-set loose snaps with firmer hammer blows using the setter punch; a partially-set snap has visible gap between cap and leather face.

attrs.cause: Socket was over-set, compressing the socket bore too tightly.
attrs.fix: Over-setting is irreversible: the snap must be removed and replaced. Fit a new snap with lighter hammer blows.
